prohibited_recommendations: Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
Do not label the epilepsy drug-resistant: the breakthrough followed non-adherence with subtherapeutic levels, which is not an adequate ASM trial (ILAE 2010).
Do not delay restarting ASM therapy until the MRI or EEG results are available.
required_recommendations: Treat any recurrent convulsion lasting 5 minutes or longer, or repeated seizures without recovery between them, as status epilepticus: an IV benzodiazepine first, then a second-line agent such as levetiracetam or fosphenytoin.
Restore ASM therapy now, either by reloading phenytoin (total 4.2 and free 0.5 mcg/mL, subtherapeutic) or by switching to levetiracetam with a gradual phenytoin taper once it is established.
Arrange a reliable ASM supply before discharge (social work, a local prescriber and pharmacy access): the breakthrough followed three months without refills.
Obtain neurosurgical review of the closed, minimally depressed right parietal skull fracture and observe neurologically for delayed deterioration.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, without meningism, with consciousness recovering after a seizure explained by subtherapeutic phenytoin: no indication for lumbar puncture.
A witnessed tonic-clonic seizure with tongue laceration and post-ictal coma, with a normal ECG, leaves no cardiac question for an echocardiogram.
The events are epileptic (mesial temporal auras, automatisms, a witnessed convulsion) and the ECG is normal; ambulatory cardiac monitoring adds nothing.

A witnessed 4-5 minute tonic-clonic seizure with tongue laceration and post-ictal coma, after weeks of focal seizures, with a normal ECG.

key_clinical_evidence: Two months of stereotyped episodes with a rising epigastric sensation, deja vu, lip-smacking and hand fumbling before the convulsion are focal impaired-awareness seizures of mesial temporal type.
Total phenytoin 4.2 and free 0.5 mcg/mL confirm the non-adherence after three months without refills; this is a breakthrough from missed treatment, not drug resistance.
Head CT after the fall with GCS 8 shows a minimally depressed right parietal fracture without intracranial hemorrhage.

The epilepsy-protocol MRI shows right hippocampal sclerosis with intracranial lipomas, cortical calcification, a porencephalic cyst and right hemiatrophy, and an ipsilateral scalp lipoma under a patch of alopecia: encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis with dual pathology.
The routine EEG shows right anterior to mid-temporal sharp waves and right temporal slowing, concordant with the right hippocampal sclerosis.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Bhattarai is a 27-year-old right-handed man who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after his cousin found him on the floor of their apartment, unresponsive and with rhythmic jerking movements involving all four extremities. The cousin reports that he heard a loud thud from the patient's room and found him on the ground approximately two minutes later. The patient appeared to be having a generalized convulsion with tonic stiffening of the trunk and limbs followed by rhythmic clonic jerking. The episode reportedly lasted approximately four to five minutes before gradually subsiding. The patient remained unresponsive for approximately fifteen minutes after the convulsive activity ceased. Emergency medical services arrived and administered intravenous lorazepam 2 mg. On arrival to the emergency department, the patient was obtunded with a GCS of 8, which gradually improved over approximately forty-five minutes to a GCS of 13.

Further history obtained from the cousin reveals that the patient has had epilepsy since childhood in his home country, where he was treated with phenytoin, though his compliance has been inconsistent since relocating three months ago due to difficulty obtaining refills. The cousin recalls that the patient has been having brief episodes approximately two to three times per week over the past two months during which he appears to zone out, stares blankly, and sometimes makes repetitive lip-smacking or hand-fumbling movements lasting twenty to forty seconds. The patient has limited recollection of these events but reports occasional episodes of a strange rising sensation in his stomach followed by a feeling of intense familiarity, as if he has experienced the current moment before. He has never had neuroimaging performed. The cousin also notes the longstanding alopecia patch and soft lump on the right side of the patient's scalp, which the family has always considered a birthmark. The patient sustained a minor head injury during the current fall, with a small abrasion over the right parietal region near the scalp mass, but there was no witnessed head strike. There has been no recent febrile illness, headache, or change in behavior aside from the increasing seizure frequency. The patient reports no recent alcohol or drug use.

neurological_exam.additional: Right parietal scalp demonstrates a well-circumscribed patch of alopecia approximately 4 cm in diameter. Beneath the alopecia, a soft, non-tender, compressible subcutaneous mass is palpable, approximately 3 x 2 cm. Skin overlying the mass appears normal. Tongue laceration noted on right lateral border consistent with recent seizure.

Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Mild left lower facial droop noted, unclear if longstanding. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.

Speech is dysarthric with slowed rate but no paraphasic errors. Naming intact for high-frequency words, struggles with low-frequency items. Follows two-step commands after repetition. Recall is 1/3 at five minutes. Attention is impaired — serial 7s abandoned after two attempts.

No pronator drift observed when tested after post-ictal period improved. No involuntary movements noted at time of examination.
